newsitem.title: USA: Army may push reluctant witness to talk in sex case.
newsitem.headline: Army may push reluctant witness to talk in sex case.

text.p: An Army officer overseeing a sexual misconduct case against the Army's top enlisted man said on Monday he might seek to have the defendant's original accuser recalled to active duty to force her to testify.

Meanwhile, one of her fellow accusers broke down in court, barely holding back tears, upon describing how she became ostracized in her office after accusing the Sergeant Major of the Army, Gene McKinney, of making a series of unwanted sexual propositions.

The original accuser who started the case rolling against McKinney, Sgt. Maj. Brenda Hoster, has retired from active duty and is refusing to testify in the hearing under way to determine whether McKinney will be court-martialed.

McKinney, 46, faces 18 charges including indecent assault, adultery and obstruction of justice and could be jailed for 45 years if convicted on all counts. His case is the latest embarrassment to the Army in a series of sex scandals that have ruined the careers of high-profile service people.

Col. Robert Jarvis, the investigating officer in the hearing, a position akin to judge, told lawyers in the case he might ask the Army to recall Hoster to active duty to force her to testify. Secretary of the Army Togo West, a civilian, would have the final decision.
"I will let everyone know that I am pursuing that," Jarvis told lawyers in the hearing.
McKinney's civilian lawyer, Charles Gittins, later told reporters he was surprised by the move.
"I frankly don't hold out much hope that the Army leadership would have the courage to take a bold step like that," Gittins told reporters.
Gittins said he suspected Hoster was reluctant to testify because she knows that he will attempt to discredit her.

The Army has no authority to force civilians or retired soldiers to testify in this kind of preliminary hearing, which is similar to a grand jury investigation in civilian court. But Hoster could be subpoenaed in a court-martial.
Hoster first brought sexual misconduct accusations against McKinney in February upon learning that he had been named to a high-level panel on sexual harassment in the military.

After Hoster came forward, three other service women also reported incidents with McKinney. One Army sergeant said McKinney pressured her into unwanted sex while she was nearly eight months pregant. A third said he groped her from within his Pentagon office.
The third accuser, Navy Petty Officer Johanna M. Vinson, testified on Monday that McKinney made a series of sexual propositions when the two met at a conference in Denver.
Vinson said she decided against filing a formal complaint because she considered it an isolated incident and possibly a misguided search for compassion after McKinney's son died from a road accident.
But after Hoster made her story public, Vinson said she decided to come forward and that this brought difficulties with co-workers.
"People I thought I knew I don't know. People are judging me," she said, raising her hand to her mouth as her voice cracked with emotion.
Vinson said her life was made even worse when a Washington newspaper printed a story quoting a colleague who alleged Vinson was prone to making up stories.
McKinney's wife, Wilhemina, watched intently from the gallery with pursed lips as Vinson described how McKinney repeatedly asked her up to his hotel room.
Other alleged victims have testified in graphic detail that McKinney made aggressive physical advances and bragged about his love-making skills.
